concept.name: Bear put spread
concept.definition: A bear put spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long put at a higher strike and a short put at a lower strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate decline in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry.
concept.intuition: You buy downside protection/participation but sell away the extreme-crash part to make the bearish bet cheaper.
concept.mechanics: Net debit at entry; maximum loss = debit above the higher strike; maximum gain = (strike width - debit) at or below the lower strike. It is the debit-spread counterpart of the bear call spread.
concept.formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K2 - net debit, where K1 < K2 are the put strikes.
concept.failure_modes: Because of downside skew, the long higher-strike put is often expensively priced relative to the short leg, raising breakevens; the capped payoff misses the bulk of true crash payoffs that outright puts capture.
concept.misconceptions: A bear put spread is not equivalent to shorting stock with limited risk — it decays with time and needs the decline to happen before expiration to profit fully.
concept.example: Buy the XYZ $100 put for $4, sell the $95 put for $1.50: debit $2.50. At or below $95 the spread is worth $5 (gain $250); at or above $100 the debit is lost.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
